doc.title: Manuel "Fess" Manetta and Edward "Kid" Ory Interview, 1958-08-26

title: The rare Sunshine records and Rip Spikes
summary: The records now sell for $90; Ory tells how Rip Spikes lost the masters, and they discuss the brothers' later fates.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

And then I went to Spikes Brothers and Dink and all. And then I went to Spikes Brothers and Dink and all. Dink died, you know, a couple years ago. Yes. About four years, I guess. Yeah, I heard. And the record went up to $90 a piece. Dr. Extra paid $90 for his income.

And when it started going up, I heard about it. It was selling for $35 and kept going up. So I went to Spikes, Rip Spikes. And I said, Rip, what happened to the master record, the Sunshine Label? I recorded it. You want to sell them? I haven't got them. He said, well, we sold the house and we left them in the garage and the people threw them in the alley. And then when I told him what happened, how the record was selling, you know, what people were getting for them, boy, he didn't know what to say. But I wasn't going to tell them until I buy them from him and get a receipt, you know.
But the Spike brothers all dead now? Both brothers dead? I know.
I know. I saw where Johnny died, the piano player. I think Rip is still living here around Los Angeles. And where it...
Yeah, Rip had a band that recorded later for Columbia, didn't he? Was that his own band, Bill? Rip Spikes?
Must have been. Must have been. He's never seen one record about 1927 or so.
Well, he's been there. Could have been Los Angeles. Yeah.
